cues.text: MIT 8107, Software Development Lifecycle.
Study Session 6: Project Documentation and Team Collaboration.
Chapter one: Documentation throughout the SDLC.
Let's begin with a simple question.
When a software project is running, where does everything the team knows actually live?
If the answer is only "in people's heads," the project is in trouble.
That is why we study project documentation.
Project documentation records the purpose of the project, its requirements, the decisions that were made, the design, the implementation, the quality evidence, the deployment, and the operation.
Notice how that list follows the whole life of the system, from the first idea through to running it day to day.
And it does real work.
It supports shared understanding across the team.
It supports onboarding, which means helping new people become productive.
It supports traceability, which is the ability to follow a thread from one artefact to another.
It supports maintenance, governance, and continuity.
Now, what makes documentation good?
The source gives us a clear list.
Documentation should be accurate.
It should be appropriate for its audience.
It should be current.
It should be searchable.
It should be versioned.
It should be accessible to authorised users.
And it should be maintained with the work, not left behind it.
There is a balance here, and the source names both ways to fail.
Over-documentation creates stale bureaucracy: piles of documents nobody updates and nobody trusts.
Insufficient documentation creates key-person risk and ambiguity.
Key-person risk means the project depends on one individual who holds the knowledge, so if that person leaves, the knowledge leaves too.
And a related point about Agile: Agile values useful documentation, not no documentation.
Agile does not say "write nothing." It says write what is useful.
Next, a table.
It has two columns, Stage and Documents and purpose, and it walks through the SDLC in eight stages.
Let's go row by row, in order.
First row, Initiation.
The documents here are the business case, the charter, the scope, the stakeholders, and feasibility.
These establish why the project exists, what it covers, who is involved, and whether it can realistically be done.
Second row, Requirements.
Here we have the BRD, which stands for business requirements document, and it captures business objectives.
Then the SRS, the software requirements specification, also written as FRD, and then user stories, acceptance criteria, and traceability.
Third row, Design.
The documents are the architecture or design specification, ADRs, which are architecture decision records, UML and ERD diagrams, API contracts, and a threat model.
Fourth row, Development.
The documents are the README, coding standards, code comments, API docs, and version history.
Fifth row, Testing.
The documents are the test plan and test cases, evidence, defect records, and coverage and acceptance.
Sixth row, Deployment.
The documents are release notes, change approval, and a migration and rollback runbook.
Seventh row, Maintenance.
The documents are the operations runbook, monitoring, incident and postmortem records, and the support or user guide.
Eighth and last row, Retirement.
The documents are migration, retention and deletion, and a decommission record.
Even when a system ends, documentation continues, because someone must record what happened to the data and the service.
Now let's separate documentation by audience.
Technical documentation serves developers and operations.
User documentation supports end users.
Project documentation supports governance and coordination.
The same system needs all three, but each is written for a different reader.
Let's look at requirements more closely.
A good requirement has an ID, a description, a rationale, acceptance criteria, a priority, an owner, and a change history.
The ID lets everyone refer to it unambiguously.
The rationale says why it matters.
The acceptance criteria say how we will know it is met.
The owner is the accountable person, and the change history shows how it has evolved.
Then there is the traceability matrix.
It connects requirement, to design, to test, to release evidence.
Think of it as a chain you can follow in either direction.
Here is the source's example.
Requirement R-12 says "authorised users see own invoices." In the matrix, R-12 maps to an API access policy, to a positive test and a negative test, and to a release version.
The positive test checks that authorised users do see their own invoices, and the negative test checks the opposite case.
And here is an important qualification: missing tests identify gaps, not automatically a failed product.
If a requirement has no test, the matrix is telling you your evidence is incomplete.
It is not telling you the product is broken.
Now to the ADR, the architecture decision record.
An ADR records its status, the context, the options considered, the decision, the reasons, and the consequences.
That means future readers can see not only what was decided but why, and what alternatives were rejected.
API documentation describes endpoints, authentication, request and response formats, errors, examples, versioning, and rate limits.
OpenAPI provides machine-readable descriptions of HTTP APIs, so tools as well as people can read them.
Diagrams explain boundaries, meaning where one component or system ends and another begins.
Then there is docs-as-code.
This approach stores Markdown alongside the source code.
Updates to the documentation are reviewed in a pull request, the same way code changes are, and the documentation can be generated and published.
To keep all this healthy, the source recommends using templates, ownership, a review cadence, revision history, access control, and archival.
Templates give consistency.
Ownership means someone is responsible.
A review cadence means a regular schedule for checking.
Revision history records changes.
Access control limits who can see what.
And archival preserves older material properly.
Finally, a firm security rule.
Do not place production secrets, biometrics, or customer records in documentation or in test fixtures.
Documents get copied, shared, and indexed, so sensitive data does not belong in them, and the same goes for the sample data used in tests.
